### When a force inclusion reorders the chain [#when-a-force-inclusion-reorders-the-chain]

A force inclusion can cause a reorg on the child chain. This happens when the sequencer produced blocks it never posted to the parent chain. Those blocks were soft-confirmed through the sequencer feed, but the force-included messages now come before them in the Sequencer Inbox.

Every node that follows the sequencer feed reorgs as soon as it reads the empty batch that `forceInclusion` posts to the Sequencer Inbox. It drops the unposted blocks. Soft-confirmed transactions in those blocks can be lost for good:

- **Only an active sequencer re-sequences.** If the sequencer isn't active when the reorg happens, it doesn't re-sequence the dropped messages.
- **Re-sequencing has a depth limit.** The sequencer re-sequences up to 1,024 dropped messages by default (`node.transaction-streamer.max-reorg-resequence-depth`). It removes any messages beyond that limit.
- **Re-sequencing is best effort.** The sequencer skips any message it fails to re-sequence and moves on to the next one.
- **Re-sequenced transactions can fail.** The chain state changes underneath them, so some revert or are dropped.

> **A reorg happens on each node, not on the whole chain**
>
> Only nodes that follow the sequencer feed see the unposted blocks, so only they reorg. A node that reads only from the parent chain builds blocks from posted batches, already in canonical order. It never reorgs because of a force inclusion. It can still follow a parent-chain reorg unless you set `node.inbox-reader.read-mode` to `safe` or `finalized`, which also turns off the feed. In exchange, it sees transactions only after they're posted, not when they're soft-confirmed.

### How the Censorship Timeout shortens the window [#how-the-censorship-timeout-shortens-the-window]

The force-inclusion window is the smaller of `delayBlocks` and the delay buffer. Arbitrum One and Arbitrum Nova both have the delay buffer enabled.

- **The buffer starts full.** The maximum is 14,400 Ethereum blocks (48 hours). While the buffer is at least `delayBlocks`, the window is `delayBlocks`: 24 hours on Arbitrum One and 24 hours on Arbitrum Nova.
- **Long delays drain the buffer.** If the sequencer delays a Delayed Inbox message past a `threshold`, the extra delay comes out of the buffer. The `threshold` is 150 blocks (30 minutes) on Arbitrum One and 300 blocks (1 hour) on Arbitrum Nova.
- **Draining is capped and applied later.** The contract records a delay when it updates the buffer and deducts it at the next update. Each deduction is at most the number of blocks between the two updates.
- **The buffer never drops below the threshold.** So the shortest possible window is 30 minutes on Arbitrum One and 1 hour on Arbitrum Nova.
- **The buffer refills slowly.** At each update, the contract adds 5% of the blocks elapsed since the last update, then deducts any recorded delay. That is about one day of buffer for every 20 days without long delays.

The first force-included message of an outage gets the full `delayBlocks` window, as long as the buffer holds at least `delayBlocks` when the outage starts. That force inclusion records a delay of about `delayBlocks` blocks. Later messages in the same long outage pay for it, so their windows get shorter. Repeated outages drain the buffer the same way. For the full math, see the [`DelayBuffer` library](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/nitro-contracts/blob/4341b132cfbdcc980ead03765ca5224ff6cb5d97/src/bridge/DelayBuffer.sol) and the [Censorship Timeout](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/sequencer#censorship-timeout) section.

### Window settings on Arbitrum One and Arbitrum Nova [#window-settings-on-arbitrum-one-and-arbitrum-nova]

Block counts are Ethereum blocks, at 12 seconds per block.

| Setting                               | Arbitrum One                                                                                              | Arbitrum Nova                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `delayBlocks`, the longest window     | 7200 blocks (24 hours) | 7200 blocks (24 hours) |
| Largest delay buffer                  | 14,400 blocks (48 hours)                                                                                  | 14,400 blocks (48 hours)                                                                              |
| `threshold`, also the shortest window | 150 blocks (30 minutes)                                                                                   | 300 blocks (1 hour)                                                                                   |
| Buffer refill rate                    | 5% of elapsed blocks                                                                                      | 5% of elapsed blocks                                                                                  |

To get the deadline for a message, call [`forceInclusionDeadline(blockNumber)`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/nitro-contracts/blob/4341b132cfbdcc980ead03765ca5224ff6cb5d97/src/bridge/SequencerInbox.sol#L755-L764) on the Sequencer Inbox. It applies the buffer's pending changes for you. You can force-include from the block after the deadline it returns.

The deadline can move. A sequencer batch or another force inclusion updates the buffer, which changes the result. Call `forceInclusionDeadline` again right before you call `forceInclusion`.

## Force-include a signed transaction with the Arbitrum SDK [#force-include-a-signed-transaction-with-the-arbitrum-sdk]

These steps send a signed child-chain transaction with `sendL2Message` and force-include it. To force-include another message type, replace steps 2 and 3 with that type's [Inbox function](#what-you-can-force-include). Steps 4 and 5 work the same for every type. Step 6 finds the result by the signed transaction's hash, so it applies only to signed transactions.

The steps use the [`InboxTools`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/arbitrum-sdk/blob/cbb96c6f7f84d71bdef65d0fd9d3d7275a236711/packages/sdk/src/lib/inbox/inbox.ts#L64) class from `@arbitrum/sdk` v4 with ethers v5.

You need:

- An account with ETH on the parent chain to pay for the parent-chain transactions.
- The same account with enough funds on the child chain to pay for the child-chain transaction.
- An RPC endpoint for the parent chain.
- An RPC endpoint for a child-chain node that reads from the parent chain. A full node works. It doesn't need the sequencer or the sequencer feed.

### 1. Set up the SDK [#1-set-up-the-sdk]

```ts
import { providers, Wallet, Contract, utils } from 'ethers';
import { getArbitrumNetwork, InboxTools } from '@arbitrum/sdk';

const parentProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(process.env.PARENT_CHAIN_RPC);
const childProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(process.env.CHAIN_RPC);

const parentWallet = new Wallet(process.env.PRIVATE_KEY, parentProvider);
const childWallet = new Wallet(process.env.PRIVATE_KEY, childProvider);

const childNetwork = await getArbitrumNetwork(childProvider);
const inboxTools = new InboxTools(parentWallet, childNetwork);
```

`getArbitrumNetwork` knows Arbitrum One, Arbitrum Nova, and Arbitrum Sepolia out of the box. If your chain is not one of them, call `registerCustomArbitrumNetwork` with your chain's details first. Otherwise, `getArbitrumNetwork` throws `Unrecognized network`.

### 2. Sign the child-chain transaction [#2-sign-the-child-chain-transaction]

`signChildTx` fills in the nonce and fees from the child-chain node if you leave them out. It always sets the gas limit to the node's current estimate, with no margin. Then it signs the transaction with your child-chain wallet.

```ts
const feeData = await childProvider.getFeeData();

const signedTx = await inboxTools.signChildTx(
  {
    to: '0xRecipientAddress',
    value: utils.parseEther('0.01'),
    data: '0x',
    // Leave room for the base fee to rise before the transaction executes
    maxFeePerGas: feeData.maxFeePerGas.mul(3),
    maxPriorityFeePerGas: 0,
  },
  childWallet,
);

// Save this hash to find the transaction on the child chain later
const childTxHash = utils.parseTransaction(signedTx).hash;
```

The fee cap and gas limit are fixed once you sign. Your transaction might execute a day or more later, so set `maxFeePerGas` well above today's base fee. If the transaction's gas use depends on chain state that can change, sign it with ethers directly and set a higher gas limit yourself.

### 3. Send it to the Delayed Inbox [#3-send-it-to-the-delayed-inbox]

`sendChildSignedTx` calls `sendL2Message` on the Delayed Inbox. Because the message is signed, the child chain executes it from your own address, with no [address aliasing](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l1-to-l2-messaging#address-aliasing).

```ts
const parentTx = await inboxTools.sendChildSignedTx(signedTx);
const parentReceipt = await parentTx.wait();
```

If the sequencer is running, it adds your transaction without force inclusion. Skip to step 6.

### 4. Wait for the force-inclusion deadline [#4-wait-for-the-force-inclusion-deadline]

Ask the Sequencer Inbox for your message's deadline. The result includes pending changes in the delay buffer.

```ts
const sequencerInbox = new Contract(childNetwork.ethBridge.sequencerInbox, ['function forceInclusionDeadline(uint64 blockNumber) view returns (uint64)'], parentProvider);

const deadline = await sequencerInbox.forceInclusionDeadline(parentReceipt.blockNumber);
console.log(`Force inclusion opens after parent-chain block ${deadline}`);
```

Wait until the parent chain's block number is greater than `deadline`. Then check the deadline again, because a later batch can move it.

If your parent chain is an Arbitrum chain, both numbers are Ethereum block numbers, not the parent chain's own block numbers. The plain ethers receipt doesn't include the Ethereum block number. Read both numbers through the SDK's `ArbitrumProvider` instead:

```ts
import { ArbitrumProvider } from '@arbitrum/sdk';

const arbParentProvider = new ArbitrumProvider(parentProvider);

// The Ethereum block number your message was recorded at
const messageReceipt = await arbParentProvider.getTransactionReceipt(parentReceipt.transactionHash);
const l3Deadline = await sequencerInbox.forceInclusionDeadline(messageReceipt.l1BlockNumber);

// Compare against this, not against parentProvider.getBlockNumber()
const currentBlock = await arbParentProvider.getBlock('latest');
const isOpen = currentBlock.l1BlockNumber > l3Deadline.toNumber();
```

### 5. Force-include the message [#5-force-include-the-message]

Pass your own message to `forceInclude`. Take the `MessageDelivered` event from your step 3 receipt, and read the message's accumulator from the Bridge contract.

```ts
import { ParentTransactionReceipt } from '@arbitrum/sdk';

const bridge = new Contract(childNetwork.ethBridge.bridge, ['function delayedInboxAccs(uint256 index) view returns (bytes32)'], parentProvider);

// The MessageDelivered event your step 3 transaction emitted
const [delivered] = new ParentTransactionReceipt(parentReceipt).getMessageDeliveredEvents();

const forceTx = await inboxTools.forceInclude({
  event: delivered,
  blockNumber: parentReceipt.blockNumber,
  blockHash: parentReceipt.blockHash,
  delayedAcc: await bridge.delayedInboxAccs(delivered.messageIndex),
} as any); // forceInclude reads only these fields
await forceTx.wait();
```

The call includes your message and every earlier message still waiting. If your parent chain is an Arbitrum chain, `forceInclude` converts the block number to an Ethereum block number for you. If the sequencer or someone else already included your message, the call reverts with `DelayedBackwards`.

> **Calling forceInclude() with no arguments can miss your message**
>
> With no arguments, `forceInclude` searches the parent chain for the newest eligible message. The search is stricter than the contract:
>
> - It treats a message as eligible only after both `delayBlocks` and `delaySeconds` have passed.
> - It ignores the delay buffer. If the buffer has shortened the window, it misses messages the contract already accepts.
> - It searches back at most 19,635 blocks (`3 * 6545`, about three days) from the newest eligible block. It misses older messages.
>
> In these cases it returns `null`, even though your window is open. Use the no-argument form only when you don't have your message's receipt.

### 6. Confirm the transaction on the child chain [#6-confirm-the-transaction-on-the-child-chain]

The child-chain node reads the force-included message from the Sequencer Inbox and processes it. Wait with a timeout, because an invalid transaction never gets a receipt.

```ts
// Wait up to 30 minutes for one confirmation
const childReceipt = await childProvider.waitForTransaction(childTxHash, 1, 30 * 60 * 1000).catch(() => null);

if (childReceipt === null) {
  console.log('No receipt. ArbOS may have dropped the transaction; see "When a signed transaction has no receipt".');
} else {
  console.log(`Child-chain status: ${childReceipt.status === 1 ? 'success' : 'reverted'}`);
}
```

For other message types, start from the same step 3 receipt. Wrap it with `new ParentTransactionReceipt(parentReceipt)`, then:

- **ETH deposit.** Call `getEthDeposits(childProvider)`, then `wait()` on the result.
- **Retryable ticket.** Call `getParentToChildMessages(childProvider)`, then `waitForStatus()` on the result.

### Withdraw ETH while the sequencer is down [#withdraw-eth-while-the-sequencer-is-down]

To move ETH back to the parent chain without the sequencer, force-include a call to the `ArbSys` precompile's `withdrawEth` method. [`ArbSys`](/arbitrum-essentials/precompiles/reference#arbsys) lives at address `0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000064`.

In step 2, sign this transaction instead:

```ts
const arbSys = new utils.Interface(['function withdrawEth(address destination) payable returns (uint256)']);

const signedTx = await inboxTools.signChildTx(
  {
    to: '0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000064',
    // The ETH to withdraw from your child-chain balance
    value: utils.parseEther('0.1'),
    // The parent-chain address that receives the ETH
    data: arbSys.encodeFunctionData('withdrawEth', [parentWallet.address]),
    maxFeePerGas: feeData.maxFeePerGas.mul(3),
    maxPriorityFeePerGas: 0,
  },
  childWallet,
);
```

Then follow steps 3 through 6. When the transaction lands, the child chain burns your ETH and creates a child-to-parent message. Claim the ETH on the parent chain after the challenge period: 6.4 days on Arbitrum One and 6.4 days on Arbitrum Nova. See [Withdrawing ETH](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/withdraw/eth-and-messages#withdrawing-eth) for the claim steps.

- [`delayedInbox-l2msg`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/arbitrum-tutorials/tree/master/packages/delayedInbox-l2msg) sends a signed transaction through the Delayed Inbox while the sequencer is running.
- [`force-inclusion`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/arbitrum-tutorials/tree/master/packages/force-inclusion) deploys a test chain with a 90-second window, deposits ETH, and force-includes the deposit with no sequencer.

## When a signed transaction has no receipt [#when-a-signed-transaction-has-no-receipt]

Force inclusion guarantees that every child-chain node processes your message. It does not guarantee that a signed transaction executes. ArbOS checks a signed transaction before it executes it. If a check fails, ArbOS drops the transaction, and the transaction hash never gets a receipt.

| What went wrong                                                                               | Result                            |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| The nonce no longer matches, because you sent another transaction from the same account first | Dropped, no receipt               |
| The child chain's base fee rose above your `maxFeePerGas`                                     | Dropped, no receipt               |
| Your child-chain balance cannot cover the gas limit times the fee, plus the value             | Dropped, no receipt               |
| The signature or chain ID is wrong, or the message cannot be parsed                           | Dropped, no receipt               |
| The transaction passes these checks but runs out of gas or reverts                            | Included, receipt with `status` 0 |

If you get no receipt, check the account's current nonce and balance on the child chain. Compare the current base fee with the fee cap you signed. Then sign a new transaction and resend it. ArbOS records the reason only in the node's log, at debug level, or at warn level on a chain in debug mode.

## Things to consider [#things-to-consider]

- **A signed transaction's nonce is fixed when you sign.** Wait until the forced transaction lands before you send another child-chain transaction from the same account.
- **A signed transaction's fee cap and gas limit are fixed when you sign.** Set both with room to spare, as described in step 2.
- **You pay parent-chain gas twice.** You pay once to send the message and again for `forceInclusion`. Signed transactions, unsigned messages, and retryable tickets also pay child-chain gas.
- **An Inbox allowlist limits who can send.** A chain owner can turn on the Inbox allowlist with `setAllowListEnabled`. The Inbox then checks the account that signed the parent-chain transaction (`tx.origin`), so only allowlisted accounts can send messages to the Delayed Inbox. Other accounts cannot start a forced transaction.
- **A paused Inbox accepts no messages.** The chain owner can pause the Inbox, and every send function reverts while it is paused. Messages already in the Delayed Inbox can still be force-included, because `forceInclusion` is on the Sequencer Inbox. See [Ownership and access](/launch-arbitrum-chain/operate/ownership-and-access#inbox-delayed-inbox).
- **Each chain sets its own window.** The numbers on this page are for Arbitrum One and Arbitrum Nova. If you run your own Arbitrum chain, it can use different values. See [Sequencer timing adjustments](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/sequencer/sequencer-timing-adjustments).

## Example scenario [#example-scenario]

Suppose the Arbitrum One sequencer goes offline while its delay buffer is full.

1. **Monday, 12:00 UTC.** You send a signed transaction to the Delayed Inbox. The parent chain records it in Ethereum block `N`.
2. **Monday, 18:00 UTC.** The sequencer is still offline. A call to `forceInclusion` reverts with `ForceIncludeBlockTooSoon`.
3. **Tuesday, about 12:00 UTC.** Ethereum reaches the block after `N` + 7200. You call `forceInclusion`, and your message enters the Sequencer Inbox.
4. **Tuesday, a few minutes later.** Child-chain full nodes read the new inbox entry and process your transaction. If it passes the ArbOS checks, your receipt appears on the child chain.
5. **Later.** The sequencer comes back online. It continues from the force-included messages. Every node that follows the sequencer feed has already dropped the blocks the sequencer produced but never posted, and the sequencer tries to re-sequence them.

If the sequencer had come back on Monday evening, it would have included your message, and you wouldn't have needed step 3.

# Monitor withdrawals programmatically (/arbitrum-bridge/withdrawal-monitoring)

This page is intended for chain operators and integration partners (exchanges, bridges, infrastructure providers) who need to track withdrawals programmatically and be alerted when one gets stuck. To trace a single transaction end to end, see [Tracing bridge transactions](/arbitrum-bridge/bridge-transaction-traceability). To initiate withdrawals from code, see [Withdraw ETH and messages](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/withdraw/eth-and-messages). To learn the protocol-level background, see [Child-to-parent messaging](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l2-to-l1-messaging).

A withdrawal from an Arbitrum chain is a child chain-to-parent chain message that passes through several protocol stages before funds are claimable. Most "where is my withdrawal?" questions come down to not knowing which stage a withdrawal is in, or how long each stage is expected to take on a given chain. This guide maps the lifecycle to observable onchain state and to the [`@arbitrum/sdk`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/arbitrum-sdk) status model, gives expected timelines per chain type, and provides tested code for monitoring one withdrawal or indexing many.

## The withdrawal lifecycle [#the-withdrawal-lifecycle]

Every withdrawal—whether a token withdrawal through the bridge UI or a raw `ArbSys.sendTxToL1` call—moves through the same stages:

| Stage            | What happens onchain                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | SDK status    |
| :--------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------ |
| **1. Initiated** | The child chain transaction calls the [`ArbSys`](/arbitrum-essentials/precompiles/reference#arbsys) precompile (directly, or via a token gateway), which emits an `L2ToL1Tx` event containing the withdrawal's `position` | `UNCONFIRMED` |
| **2. Batched**   | The sequencer posts the batch containing the transaction to the parent chain (typically within minutes)                                                                                                                            | `UNCONFIRMED` |
| **3. Asserted**  | A validator posts an assertion covering the withdrawal's child chain block (`AssertionCreated` event on the Rollup contract)                                                                                                   | `UNCONFIRMED` |
| **4. Confirmed** | After the challenge period passes without a successful challenge, the assertion is confirmed (`AssertionConfirmed` event); the Rollup contract registers the assertion's send root in the outbox (`SendRootUpdated` event) | `CONFIRMED`   |
| **5. Executed**  | Someone calls `Outbox.executeTransaction()` with a Merkle proof (obtained from a child chain node via `NodeInterface.constructOutboxProof()`);; the outbox marks the withdrawal spent (`OutBoxTransactionExecuted` event) and releases the funds                                       | `EXECUTED`    |

Two properties of this lifecycle cause most confusion:

- **Execution is manual.** Confirmation makes a withdrawal _claimable_; it doesn't deliver funds. Someone (the user through the bridge UI's **Claim** button, or your infrastructure) must execute the claim on the parent chain. A withdrawal can sit in `CONFIRMED` indefinitely. To learn why the protocol works this way, see [Why child to parent chain messages require manual execution](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l2-to-l1-messaging#why-child-to-parent-chain-messages-require-manual-execution).
- **Time-to-claimable is more than the challenge period.** The clock users care about includes batch posting (minutes) _plus_ waiting for the next assertion to cover their block (up to the chain's assertion posting interval, commonly up to an hour) _plus_ the challenge period after that assertion is created. On a chain with [fast withdrawals](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/validation/fast-withdrawals), the committee's confirmation frequency replaces the challenge period wait, but batch posting and assertion cadence still apply—which is why a "15-minute fast withdrawal chain" can legitimately take an hour or more to reach claimable.

### Mapping bridge UI phases to protocol states [#mapping-bridge-ui-phases-to-protocol-states]

The [Arbitrum bridge UI](https://bridge.arbitrum.io/) presents a withdrawal as three user-facing steps, and support conversations often reference them as "phases." They map to the lifecycle above as follows:

| Bridge UI step                                     | Lifecycle stages                               | SDK status               |
| :------------------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------- | :----------------------- |
| Phase 1 — withdrawal submitted                     | Initiated                                      | `UNCONFIRMED`            |
| Phase 2 — countdown or waiting                     | Batched → Asserted → challenge period elapsing | `UNCONFIRMED`            |
| Phase 3 — **Claim** button available, then claimed | Confirmed → Executed                           | `CONFIRMED` → `EXECUTED` |

A withdrawal "stuck between phase 2 and phase 3" is a withdrawal that stayed `UNCONFIRMED` past its expected time-to-claimable: either no assertion covering its block exists yet, or the covering assertion hasn't been confirmed. The [diagnosis table](#diagnose-stuck-withdrawals) below separates those cases.

## Expected timelines by chain type [#expected-timelines-by-chain-type]

The dominant term in time-to-claimable is the challenge period, set by the chain's `confirmPeriodBlocks` parameter and measured in parent chain blocks. Values for Arbitrum's own chains:

| Chain configuration                                                                                   | Challenge period                                                                                      | Typical time-to-claimable                                                                                     |
| :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Arbitrum One (Rollup)                                                  | 45818 blocks ≈ 6.4 days         | ~7 days (batch + assertion cadence + challenge period)                                                        |
| Arbitrum Nova (AnyTrust) | 45818 blocks ≈ 6.4 days             | ~7 days—AnyTrust changes data availability, **not** the challenge period                                      |
| Arbitrum chain with fast withdrawals                               | Bypassed by unanimous committee confirmation                                                          | As low as ~15 minutes on BoLD-enabled chains, plus batch posting and assertion cadence |
| Arbitrum Sepolia (testnet)                                                                            | 20 blocks ≈ 4.0 minutes | Minutes                                                                                                       |

Additional timing facts your alerting thresholds should account for:

- **A challenged assertion takes longer.** If an assertion acquires a rival, confirmation waits for the challenge to resolve (bounded by the challenge period) plus a grace period (14,400 parent chain blocks ≈ 48 hours on Arbitrum One's configuration) before the winner can be confirmed. Under BoLD, an honest withdrawal is delayed by at most one additional challenge period even during a dispute—see [Assertions](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/assertions).
- **Time-to-funds = time-to-claimable + execution.** Budget for the claim transaction separately; nothing executes it automatically.

- **Custom chains choose their own values.** Read `confirmPeriodBlocks()` from the chain's Rollup contract (shown [below](#query-assertion-and-outbox-state-onchain)) rather than assuming the defaults. To learn how operators configure this, see [Customizable challenge period](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/validation/challenge-period).

## Withdrawals from an L3 [#withdrawals-from-an-l3]

A withdrawal from an L3 (an Arbitrum chain that settles on Arbitrum One or another child chain) to Ethereum is **two sequential child-to-parent withdrawals**: L3 → L2, then L2 → L1. Each leg has its own challenge period—by default 45818 parent chain blocks (≈ 6.4 days) per leg on mainnet configurations—and each leg's claim must execute before the next leg can begin. The worst case with default settings is therefore roughly two weeks end to end.

Monitor each leg independently with the same code from this guide, pointing the provider pair at the relevant chains (L3 + L2 for the first leg, L2 + L1 for the second).

Chain operators have three options for reducing the delay:

| Option                                                                                           | Time-to-claimable                                  | Trade-off                                                                                                                                 |
| :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Fast withdrawals](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/validation/fast-withdrawals)              | Down to ~15 minutes per leg on BoLD-enabled chains | Adds a committee trust assumption (unanimous validator committee); recommended primarily for AnyTrust chains where the DAC already exists |
| [Customizable challenge period](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/validation/challenge-period) | Whatever `confirmPeriodBlocks` is set to           | Shrinks the window in which fraud can be challenged; weakens the chain's security model                                                   |
| Third-party liquidity bridges                                                                    | Minutes                                            | Users receive funds from a liquidity provider rather than the canonical bridge; adds provider trust and fees; per-asset liquidity limits  |

## Monitor withdrawals with the SDK [#monitor-withdrawals-with-the-sdk]

The [`@arbitrum/sdk`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/arbitrum-sdk) (v4, ethers v5) exposes the lifecycle through `ChildToParentMessage` objects and the `ChildToParentMessageStatus` enum, whose three values match the lifecycle table above: `UNCONFIRMED` (0), `CONFIRMED` (1), and `EXECUTED` (2). The SDK handles both current (BoLD) and legacy assertion models automatically, so the same code works across chains.

Arbitrum One, Nova, and Arbitrum Sepolia are pre-registered in the SDK. For any other Arbitrum chain, register it first—all required parameters can be derived from the chain's Rollup contract address:

```ts
import { providers } from 'ethers';
import { registerCustomArbitrumNetwork, getArbitrumNetworkInformationFromRollup } from '@arbitrum/sdk';

const parentProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(PARENT_RPC_URL);

const rollupData = await getArbitrumNetworkInformationFromRollup(ROLLUP_ADDRESS, parentProvider);

registerCustomArbitrumNetwork({
  chainId: CHILD_CHAIN_ID,
  name: 'my-arbitrum-chain',
  parentChainId: rollupData.parentChainId,
  ethBridge: rollupData.ethBridge,
  confirmPeriodBlocks: rollupData.confirmPeriodBlocks,
  isCustom: true,
  isTestnet: false,
});
```

### Check the status of a withdrawal [#check-the-status-of-a-withdrawal]

Given the withdrawal's child chain transaction hash:

```ts
import { providers } from 'ethers';
import { ChildTransactionReceipt, ChildToParentMessageStatus } from '@arbitrum/sdk';

const withdrawalTxHash = WITHDRAWAL_TX_HASH;

const parentProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(PARENT_RPC_URL);
const childProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(CHILD_RPC_URL);

async function main() {
  const receipt = await childProvider.getTransactionReceipt(withdrawalTxHash);
  const childReceipt = new ChildTransactionReceipt(receipt);
  const messages = await childReceipt.getChildToParentMessages(parentProvider);
  const message = messages[0];

  const status = await message.status(childProvider);
  console.log('Status:', ChildToParentMessageStatus[status]);

  if (status === ChildToParentMessageStatus.UNCONFIRMED) {
    // Estimated parent chain block at which the withdrawal becomes executable
    const firstExecutableBlock = await message.getFirstExecutableBlock(childProvider);
    console.log('Estimated first executable parent chain block:', firstExecutableBlock.toString());
  }
}
main();
```

`getFirstExecutableBlock()` returns an estimate of the parent chain block at which the message becomes claimable (based on the covering assertion's creation block plus the challenge period), or `null` once the message is already `CONFIRMED` or `EXECUTED`. Comparing it against the parent chain's current block number gives you a countdown you can surface to users—the same countdown the bridge UI shows.

### Wait for confirmation and execute the claim [#wait-for-confirmation-and-execute-the-claim]

`waitUntilReadyToExecute()` polls until the message leaves `UNCONFIRMED`, then returns the terminal status. A `ChildToParentMessageWriter` (obtained by passing a parent chain _signer_ instead of a provider) can then execute the claim:

```ts
import { providers, Wallet } from 'ethers';
import { ChildTransactionReceipt, ChildToParentMessageStatus } from '@arbitrum/sdk';

const withdrawalTxHash = WITHDRAWAL_TX_HASH;

const parentProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(PARENT_RPC_URL);
const childProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(CHILD_RPC_URL);
const parentSigner = new Wallet(PRIVATE_KEY, parentProvider);

async function main() {
  const receipt = await childProvider.getTransactionReceipt(withdrawalTxHash);
  const childReceipt = new ChildTransactionReceipt(receipt);

  // Passing a signer yields ChildToParentMessageWriter instances, which can execute claims
  const messages = await childReceipt.getChildToParentMessages(parentSigner);
  const message = messages[0];

  // Polls every 30 seconds until the message leaves UNCONFIRMED.
  // On a chain with a live challenge period this call blocks for days —
  // use it in a worker, or poll status() on your own schedule instead.
  const status = await message.waitUntilReadyToExecute(childProvider, 30 * 1000);

  if (status === ChildToParentMessageStatus.CONFIRMED) {
    const executeTx = await message.execute(childProvider);
    const executeReceipt = await executeTx.wait();
    console.log('Claim executed on parent chain:', executeReceipt.transactionHash);
  } else {
    console.log('Message already executed');
  }
}
main();
```

Under the hood, `execute()` fetches the Merkle proof from the [`NodeInterface`](/arbitrum-essentials/nodeinterface/reference) and calls `Outbox.executeTransaction()` on the parent chain. It throws if the message isn't `CONFIRMED` yet. If you need the proof itself (for example, to execute through your own contracts), call `message.getOutboxProof(childProvider)`.

### Index many withdrawals [#index-many-withdrawals]

To monitor every withdrawal on a chain (for example, all withdrawals initiated through your bridge frontend), fetch `L2ToL1Tx` events in bulk instead of tracking individual transaction hashes:

```ts
import { providers } from 'ethers';
import { ChildToParentMessage, ChildToParentMessageStatus } from '@arbitrum/sdk';

const parentProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(PARENT_RPC_URL);
const childProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(CHILD_RPC_URL);

const fromBlock = START_BLOCK;
const toBlock = 'latest';

async function main() {
  const events = await ChildToParentMessage.getChildToParentEvents(childProvider, {
    fromBlock,
    toBlock,
  });
  console.log(`Found ${events.length} withdrawal(s)`);

  for (const event of events) {
    const message = ChildToParentMessage.fromEvent(parentProvider, event);
    const status = await message.status(childProvider);
    console.log(`position ${event.position.toString()} | ` + `child tx ${event.transactionHash} | ` + `destination ${event.destination} | ` + `${ChildToParentMessageStatus[status]}`);
  }
}
main();
```

`getChildToParentEvents` also accepts optional `position`, `destination`, and `hash` filters (all indexed fields of the `L2ToL1Tx` event), so you can restrict the scan to withdrawals bound for addresses you care about.

For a production monitor, a practical pattern is:

1. **Ingest**: scan `L2ToL1Tx` events in block-range windows on a schedule; store each withdrawal's `position`, transaction hash, destination, and initiation timestamp.
2. **Track**: poll `status()` for stored withdrawals that aren't `EXECUTED` yet. Withdrawals in `UNCONFIRMED` only change state when an assertion is confirmed, so polling them more often than the chain's assertion cadence adds no information; hourly is plenty on a seven-day chain.
3. **Alert**: flag any withdrawal that is `UNCONFIRMED` past your chain's expected time-to-claimable (challenge period + assertion cadence + margin), and any withdrawal sitting in `CONFIRMED` longer than you expect users to leave claims unexecuted.

## Query assertion and outbox state onchain [#query-assertion-and-outbox-state-onchain]

If you prefer raw contract calls—or want to monitor the assertion pipeline itself rather than individual messages—the same lifecycle is observable from three contracts: the `ArbSys` precompile on the child chain, and the Rollup and Outbox contracts on the parent chain. The following snippet checks every stage for one withdrawal:

```ts
import { providers, Contract } from 'ethers';

const withdrawalTxHash = WITHDRAWAL_TX_HASH;
const rollupAddress = ROLLUP_ADDRESS;

const ARBSYS_ADDRESS = '0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000064';
const NODE_INTERFACE_ADDRESS = '0x00000000000000000000000000000000000000C8';

const arbSysAbi = ['event L2ToL1Tx(address caller, address indexed destination, uint256 indexed hash, uint256 indexed position, uint256 arbBlockNum, uint256 ethBlockNum, uint256 timestamp, uint256 callvalue, bytes data)'];
const rollupAbi = ['function outbox() view returns (address)', 'function confirmPeriodBlocks() view returns (uint64)', 'event AssertionConfirmed(bytes32 indexed assertionHash, bytes32 blockHash, bytes32 sendRoot)'];
const outboxAbi = ['function roots(bytes32) view returns (bytes32)', 'function isSpent(uint256 index) view returns (bool)'];
const nodeInterfaceAbi = ['function constructOutboxProof(uint64 size, uint64 leaf) view returns (bytes32 send, bytes32 root, bytes32[] proof)'];

const parentProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(PARENT_RPC_URL);
const childProvider = new providers.JsonRpcProvider(CHILD_RPC_URL);

async function main() {
  // 1. The L2ToL1Tx event from the withdrawal transaction identifies the message
  const receipt = await childProvider.getTransactionReceipt(withdrawalTxHash);
  const arbSys = new Contract(ARBSYS_ADDRESS, arbSysAbi, childProvider);
  const l2ToL1TxTopic = arbSys.interface.getEventTopic('L2ToL1Tx');
  const event = receipt.logs.filter((log) => log.topics[0] === l2ToL1TxTopic).map((log) => arbSys.interface.parseLog(log))[0];
  const { position, arbBlockNum } = event.args;
  console.log('position (outbox leaf index):', position.toString(), '| child block:', arbBlockNum.toString());

  // 2. Latest confirmed assertion: its send root commits to all withdrawals up to
  //    the child chain block it covers
  const rollup = new Contract(rollupAddress, rollupAbi, parentProvider);
  const confirmed = await rollup.queryFilter(rollup.filters.AssertionConfirmed(), -100000);
  const latestConfirmation = confirmed[confirmed.length - 1];
  const { blockHash, sendRoot } = latestConfirmation.args;

  // 3. sendCount of that block = how many withdrawals the confirmed assertion covers
  const confirmedBlock = await childProvider.send('eth_getBlockByHash', [blockHash, false]);
  const sendCount = Number(confirmedBlock.sendCount);
  const isCovered = position.lt(sendCount);
  console.log('confirmed sendCount:', sendCount, '| withdrawal covered by confirmed assertion:', isCovered);

  // 4. The send root must be registered in the outbox for claims to succeed
  const outboxAddress = await rollup.outbox();
  const outbox = new Contract(outboxAddress, outboxAbi, parentProvider);
  const registered = (await outbox.roots(sendRoot)) !== '0x' + '0'.repeat(64);
  console.log('send root registered in outbox:', registered);

  // 5. Already claimed?
  console.log('outbox.isSpent(position):', await outbox.isSpent(position));

  // 6. Merkle proof for a manual Outbox.executeTransaction call
  const nodeInterface = new Contract(NODE_INTERFACE_ADDRESS, nodeInterfaceAbi, childProvider);
  const proofData = await nodeInterface.constructOutboxProof(sendCount, position.toNumber());
  console.log('proof root matches confirmed sendRoot:', proofData.root === sendRoot);
}
main();
```

How each check maps to the lifecycle:

- **`L2ToL1Tx`** (`ArbSys`, child chain): emitted at initiation. Its `position` is the withdrawal's leaf index in the send Merkle tree—the same `index` that `Outbox.executeTransaction()` and `Outbox.isSpent()` take, and the `leaf` argument to `NodeInterface.constructOutboxProof()`. The `destination`, `hash`, and `position` fields are indexed, so monitors can subscribe to them directly.
- **`AssertionCreated`** and **`AssertionConfirmed`** (Rollup contract, parent chain): the assertion pipeline. A withdrawal is covered once an assertion whose child chain block has `sendCount > position` exists; it is claimable once such an assertion is _confirmed_. `AssertionConfirmed` carries the confirmed `blockHash` and `sendRoot`. You can also read `latestConfirmed()` and `getAssertion()` on the Rollup contract for point-in-time checks. For an alerting-oriented view of this pipeline (assertion cadence, missed confirmations, validator health), run the [assertion monitor](/launch-arbitrum-chain/operate/monitoring#assertion-monitor).
- **`SendRootUpdated`** and **`roots`** (Outbox, parent chain): set by the Rollup contract at assertion confirmation. A claim can only succeed if the proof's root is registered in `roots`—this is the onchain meaning of "ready to execute."
- **`OutBoxTransactionExecuted`** and **`isSpent(position)`** (Outbox, parent chain): terminal state. The event's `transactionIndex` field equals the withdrawal's `position`.
- **`constructOutboxProof(size, leaf)`** (`NodeInterface`, child chain): builds the Merkle proof for a manual claim, where `size` is the confirmed block's `sendCount` and `leaf` is the withdrawal's `position`. The `NodeInterface` is a node-provided virtual contract—call it with `eth_call` against a child chain node; it doesn't exist onchain.

> **Chains on the legacy (pre-BoLD) protocol**
>
> On chains that haven't upgraded to BoLD, the Rollup contract identifies assertions by sequential node number instead of hash, and the corresponding events are `NodeCreated` and `NodeConfirmed(nodeNum, blockHash, sendRoot)`. The `ArbSys`, `Outbox`, and `NodeInterface` surfaces are unchanged, and the SDK abstracts the difference entirely.

If the parent chain is itself an Arbitrum chain (the L3 case), use the Rollup contract's `getAssertionCreationBlockForLogLookup(assertionHash)` getter to obtain block numbers suitable for event queries on the parent chain.

## Diagnose stuck withdrawals [#diagnose-stuck-withdrawals]

Work through the stages in order—each row's check assumes the previous rows passed. "Phase" refers to the [bridge UI mapping](#mapping-bridge-ui-phases-to-protocol-states) above.

| Symptom                                                                                   | Stuck at                             | What to check                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | Escalation                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `UNCONFIRMED`, and the transaction isn't in a posted batch yet                            | Batch posting (phase 2, early)       | `NodeInterface.getL1Confirmations(blockHash)` returns `0`, or `findBatchContainingBlock(blockNum)` reverts, for the withdrawal's child chain block                                                                                                                                                 | Batch poster is down or backed up—chain operator; see [batch poster troubleshooting](/launch-arbitrum-chain/operate/batch-poster-troubleshooting)                 |
| `UNCONFIRMED`, batched, but no assertion covers the block                                 | Assertion creation (phase 2)         | Latest `AssertionCreated` on the Rollup contract: does the assertion's child chain block have `sendCount > position`? No recent `AssertionCreated` events at all means the active validator isn't posting                                                                                          | Chain operator (validator or proposer health); the [assertion monitor](/launch-arbitrum-chain/operate/monitoring#assertion-monitor) alerts on this automatically                                 |
| `UNCONFIRMED`, assertion created, challenge period elapsed, still no `AssertionConfirmed` | Assertion confirmation (phase 2 → 3) | Whether the assertion has a rival (a challenge is in progress—confirmation waits for resolution plus a grace period); whether any validator is calling the confirmation function at all                                                                                                            | Chain operator; on a challenged chain, monitor the challenge and expect up to one extra challenge period plus grace period                                                                       |
| `CONFIRMED`, but the claim transaction reverts                                            | Execution (phase 3)                  | `Outbox.isSpent(position)`—`true` means it was already claimed (find the claim via the `OutBoxTransactionExecuted` event with `transactionIndex == position`); for an L3 withdrawal, confirm you're claiming the correct leg on the correct chain; re-derive the proof with `constructOutboxProof` | If the proof root isn't in `Outbox.roots` despite `CONFIRMED` status, something is inconsistent—collect the position, child chain transaction hash, and chain ID, and contact the chain operator |
| "Withdrawal is claimable, but funds never arrived"                                        | Execution (phase 3)                  | Nobody executed the claim—execution is manual. Check `isSpent(position)`; if `false`, execute via the SDK or the bridge UI's **Claim** button. For token withdrawals, funds are released by the parent chain gateway to the destination address once executed                                      | End-user cases: [bridge troubleshooting](/arbitrum-bridge/troubleshooting)                                                                                                                       |

> **Historical data availability**
>
> Ethereum consensus nodes are required to serve blob data for only 4,096 epochs (≈18 days). Monitors that reconstruct old withdrawal history need archive access: an [archive beacon endpoint for historical blobs](/run-a-node/beacon-nodes-historical-blobs) to re-derive the chain from batch data, and an archive child chain node for the event logs that `constructOutboxProof` reads. On AnyTrust chains, the equivalent concern is the Data Availability Committee's retention window. Claiming a confirmed withdrawal itself is unaffected—proofs are built from child chain logs, not blobs.

## See also [#see-also]

- [Tracing bridge transactions](/arbitrum-bridge/bridge-transaction-traceability) — follow a single deposit or withdrawal end to end
- [Withdraw ETH and messages](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/withdraw/eth-and-messages) and [Withdraw tokens](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/withdraw/tokens) — initiating withdrawals
- [Child-to-parent messaging](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l2-to-l1-messaging) and [Assertions](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/assertions) — protocol deep dives
- [Fast withdrawals](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/validation/fast-withdrawals) and [Customizable challenge period](/launch-arbitrum-chain/chain-config/validation/challenge-period) — chain owner configuration
- [Monitoring tools for your chain](/launch-arbitrum-chain/operate/monitoring) — the `arbitrum-monitoring` alerting suite
- [Exchange integration checklist](/launch-arbitrum-chain/integrations/exchange-integration-checklist) — deposit and withdrawal handling for exchanges
- [Precompiles reference](/arbitrum-essentials/precompiles/reference) (`ArbSys`) and [NodeInterface reference](/arbitrum-essentials/nodeinterface/reference) (`constructOutboxProof`)

# Post-launch deployment of deterministic contracts (/launch-arbitrum-chain/operate/post-launch-deployments)

Some forms of contract deployment rely on pre-made transactions with hardcoded gas limits designed for non-Arbitrum chains that only cover execution gas. Since Arbitrum also charges for data posting, these limits may be too low, causing transactions to fail. This page describes a safe, permissionless post-launch deployment method for such cases.

Using this approach, you can deploy contracts like `Multicall3`, the `EntryPoint` contract, or a `create2` factory to a live Arbitrum chain without needing to modify chain configuration. It leverages Arbitrum's cross-chain messaging infrastructure via the `Inbox.sendL2Message` function, which submits a pre-signed child chain transaction from the parent chain. Unlike retryable tickets, these messages incur parent chain data fees only at submission and aren’t subject to the 100,000 gas cap imposed on deterministic deployment flows.

## When to use this method [#when-to-use-this-method]

This approach is useful when:

- Your Arbitrum chain is already live.
- You want to deploy a contract at a specific address (e.g., using `create2`).
- The chain's genesis configuration did not include the contract.

Common examples include deployments of contracts like `Multicall3`, the `ERC-4337 EntryPoint` contract, or a `create2` factory/deterministic deployment proxy.
Note that if `deployFactoriesToL2` is set to `true` when calling `createRollup()`, the following contracts are deployed to the Arbitrum chain by default:

- [`Multicall3`](https://github.com/mds1/multicall3)
- [`DeterministicDeploymentProxy`](https://github.com/Zoltu/deterministic-deployment-proxy)
- [`ERC-4337 EntryPoint`](https://github.com/eth-infinitism/account-abstraction)
- [`CREATE3Deployer`](https://github.com/0xSequence/create3)

## Overview [#overview]

To deploy a contract post-launch:

#### 1. Fund the deployer address on the child chain: [#1-fund-the-deployer-address-on-the-child-chain]

Send **ETH** to the child chain address that will send the deployment transaction. Funding is possible using a retryable ticket or Parent-to-Child chain deposit.

#### 2. Create the signed child chain transaction: [#2-create-the-signed-child-chain-transaction]

Construct and sign a raw child chain transaction that performs the contract deployment (e.g., using `create2`). [`DeployHelper.sol`](https://github.com/OffchainLabs/nitro-contracts/blob/main/src/rollup/DeployHelper.sol) can be used as a reference for formatting the transaction.

#### 3. Send the message from the parent chain: [#3-send-the-message-from-the-parent-chain]

Call `Inbox.sendL2Message(bytes calldata message)` on the Arbitrum chain’s inbox contract. Provide the signed transaction as the input.

#### 4. Wait for the transaction to be executed on the child chain: [#4-wait-for-the-transaction-to-be-executed-on-the-child-chain]

The child chain will process and execute the message as a regular transaction. This flow does not use retryables, so if the transaction fails, it is not auto-retried and the nonce is consumed. This means the same transaction cannot be replayed, and a new transaction with a higher nonce must be created and submitted.

> **Warning**
>
> Make sure that the deployer address is sufficiently funded on the child chain before sending the transaction. If the transaction runs out of gas or fails for any reason, the associated nonce will be burned. This means that the contract cannot be deployed at the predetermined deterministic address, potentially breaking tooling and integrations that rely on that specific address.

## Advantages and considerations [#advantages-and-considerations]

This approach avoids parent chain data fees and bypasses the 100,000 gas limit associated with retryable tickets. It also requires no chain upgrade or restart and works on any standard Arbitrum or Arbitrum chain setup. However, failed transactions are not automatically retried since the flow bypasses retryable safety mechanisms. The sender must have enough **ETH** on child chain to cover gas costs, and the signed transaction must be valid and use the correct nonce.

# Bridging overview (/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/overview)

Token bridging and cross-chain messaging are fundamental aspects of building on Arbitrum. This page helps you find the right guide for your use case.

## Move **ETH** between chains [#move-eth-between-chains]

- **[Deposit ETH to Arbitrum](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/deposit/eth-and-messages#bridging-eth-to-a-child-chain)**: Bridge **ETH** from the parent chain to a child chain using the Inbox contract
- **[Withdraw **ETH** to Ethereum](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/withdraw/eth-and-messages#withdrawing-eth)**: Withdraw **ETH** from a child chain back to the parent chain via ArbSys

## Move ERC-20 tokens between chains [#move-erc-20-tokens-between-chains]

- **[Deposit tokens to Arbitrum](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/deposit/tokens)**: Move **ERC-20** tokens from the parent chain to the child chain
- **[Withdraw tokens to Ethereum](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/withdraw/tokens)**: Move **ERC-20** tokens from the child chain back to the parent chain

## Make my token bridgeable [#make-my-token-bridgeable]

Choose a gateway based on your token's requirements:

- **[Standard gateway](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/configure-token-gateway/standard)** (recommended): Automatic deployment of a standard **ERC-20** on Arbitrum, no configuration required
- **[Generic-custom gateway](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/configure-token-gateway/generic-custom)**: Custom functionality in your child chain token while using Arbitrum's built-in gateway
- **[Custom gateway](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/configure-token-gateway/custom)**: Specialized gateway logic for advanced use cases

## Send arbitrary cross-chain messages [#send-arbitrary-cross-chain-messages]

- **[Parent → child messaging](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/deposit/eth-and-messages#creating-retryable-tickets)**: Send messages from Ethereum to Arbitrum using retryable tickets
- **[Child → parent messaging](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/withdraw/eth-and-messages#sending-a-message-from-the-child-to-the-parent-chain)**: Send messages from Arbitrum to Ethereum via ArbSys and the Outbox

## Build on a custom gas token chain [#build-on-a-custom-gas-token-chain]

If you're working with an Arbitrum chain that uses a non-**ETH** gas token, see [Custom gas token chain bridging](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/custom-gas-token-chains) for SDK APIs and workflows.

# Quickstart: Arbitrum bridge (/arbitrum-bridge/quickstart)

This quickstart is for users who want to deposit **ETH** or any **ERC-20** tokens from a parent chain to a child chain or vice versa, using [Arbitrum’s bridge](https://bridge.arbitrum.io/). For example, from Ethereum to Arbitrum One, or from Arbitrum One to a Layer 3 Arbitrum chain.

We will walk you through the entire process step by step, providing as much detail as possible. If you feel stuck at any step, see [Arbitrum bridge: Troubleshooting](/arbitrum-bridge/troubleshooting), or contact us through our [Discord](https://discord.gg/arbitrum), and we will be happy to help you complete the process.

> **Bridging USDC?**
>
> Arbitrum One supports two distinct forms of **USDC** (native and bridged). Before you deposit, see [USDC on Arbitrum One](/arbitrum-bridge/usdc-arbitrum-one) so you receive the form you intend.

The only prerequisite for this quickstart is to have a Web3 wallet installed, such as MetaMask or OKX Wallet. If you don’t have one installed, visit the [Arbitrum portal](https://portal.arbitrum.io/?categories=wallet) for a list of available wallets to download.

## Deposit **ETH** or **ERC-20** tokens (from parent chain to child chain) [#deposit-eth-or-erc-20-tokens-from-parent-chain-to-child-chain]

### Step 1: Get some native currency [#step-1-get-some-native-currency]

You’ll need the native currency of the parent chain to bridge your assets to the destination chain. For example, if you want to bridge assets from Ethereum to Arbitrum One, you’ll need **ETH** on Ethereum to initiate the process.

There are several ways to obtain the native currency:

- Using a [supported centralized exchange](https://portal.arbitrum.io/projects?chains=arbitrum-one_arbitrum-nova&subcategories=centralized-exchanges), which allows you to purchase **ETH** and withdraw it to your wallet. Most major centralized exchanges support direct withdrawals from your centralized exchange wallet to the Arbitrum network.
- Using an [on-ramp service](https://portal.arbitrum.io/projects?chains=arbitrum-one_arbitrum-nova&subcategories=fiat-on-ramp), which allows you to purchase **ETH** and send it directly to your wallet.
- If you are using a testnet, request funds from a Sepolia or Arbitrum Sepolia [faucet](/chain-info#faucet-list).

### Step 2: Add the preferred network to your wallet [#step-2-add-the-preferred-network-to-your-wallet]

You'll also need to add the desired chain's RPC endpoint to your wallet. Here, we provide an example of how to do this using MetaMask; however, the process should be relatively similar to any other wallet.

1. First, click the MetaMask extension in your browser.
2. Click the network selector drop-down in the top-right corner.
3. Click the **Add a custom network** and then provide the information corresponding to the chain you want to send your assets to (see below).

![Add the desired destination network to your MetaMask](/img/bridge-quickstart-metamask-set-network.gif)

Below are the most common Arbitrum chains. For a more exhaustive list, please visit our [RPC endpoints and providers](/arbitrum-essentials/reference/node-providers) page.

| Parameter          | Arbitrum One                 | Arbitrum Nova | Arbitrum Sepolia (testnet)             |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Network name       | Arbitrum One                 | Arbitrum Nova                                 | Arbitrum Sepolia                       |
| RPC URL            | https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc | https://nova.arbitrum.io/rpc                  | https://sepolia-rollup.arbitrum.io/rpc |
| Chain ID           | 42161                        | 42170                                         | 421614                                 |
| Currency symbol    | **ETH**                      | **ETH**                                       | SepoliaETH                             |
| Block explorer URL | https://arbiscan.io          | https://nova.arbiscan.io/                     | https://sepolia.arbiscan.io            |

### Step 3: Initiate the deposit [#step-3-initiate-the-deposit]

To bridge your **ETH** or **ERC-20** tokens to a different chain, start by visiting [bridge.arbitrum.io](https://bridge.arbitrum.io/).

1. Connect your wallet to the bridge.
2. Ensure the **source** network is selected (from where you want to deposit your assets) at the top of the page.
3. Select the **destination** network (where you want your assets to go), e.g., Arbitrum One.

> **Warning**
>
> Note that testnets like Arbitrum Sepolia only appear if you have an established connection to the appropriate parent testnet network (Ethereum Sepolia).
>
> Also note, that when choosing the **source** or **destination** network, a pop up will appear where you can make your selection (illustrated below).

![Add the desired network to your Web3 wallet](/img/arb-bridge-getting-started-users-2.png)

![Add the desired network to your Web3 wallet](/img/arb-bridge-getting-started-users-3.png)

4. Select the token you want to bridge in the token drop-down menu.

![Select the token to bridge](/img/arb-bridge-getting-started-users-4.png)

![Select the token to bridge](/img/arb-bridge-getting-started-users-5.png)

5. Enter the amount of **ETH** or **ERC-20** tokens you want to bridge over in the **From** box.
6. Press **Move** funds.
7. Follow the additional prompts from your Web3 wallet.

> **Ensure sufficient ETH balance**
>
> Please ensure you have sufficient **ETH** in your wallet to cover the transation costs; otherwise, the Web3 wallet pop-up will not appear.

![Enter the amount of tokens to bridge](/img/arb-bridge-getting-started-users-6.png)

After you submit the transaction through your Web3 wallet, you can expect your funds to arrive on the destination chain within roughly 15-30 minutes (depending on chain congestion).

Also, ensure your wallet is set to the destination network so you can see when your funds arrive.

## Withdraw **ETH** or **ERC-20** tokens (from child chain to parent chain) [#withdraw-eth-or-erc-20-tokens-from-child-chain-to-parent-chain]

> **Seven day withdrawal period for Arbitrum One and Nova networks**
>
> Once you withdraw your funds from Arbitrum One or Nova through the Arbitrum bridge, you will have to wait for at least seven days to receive them on the Ethereum mainnet. For more details, see [Arbitrum Bridge: Troubleshooting](/arbitrum-bridge/troubleshooting#how-long-does-it-take-before-i-receive-my-funds-when-i-initiate-a-withdrawal-from-arbitrum-chains-one-and-nova). For the protocol-level reason behind the dispute window, see [Child-to-parent messaging](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l2-to-l1-messaging) and the FAQ entry on [why one week was chosen](/get-started/faq#why-was-one-week-chosen-for-arbitrum-ones-dispute-window).

To bridge your funds back to the parent chain, you must be connected to the [Arbitrum bridge](https://bridge.arbitrum.io/) with your wallet and ensure you establish a connection to the source network (from which you want to withdraw assets) at the top of the page. Then, select the destination network (where you want your assets to go), e.g., Ethereum mainnet.

> **Warning**
>
> Testnets like Arbitrum Sepolia only appear if you have an established connection to the appropriate parent testnet network (Ethereum Sepolia).

![Select the token to withdraw](/img/arb-bridge-getting-started-users-7.png)

1. Select the token you want to bridge in the token drop-down menu.
2. Enter the amount of **ETH** or **ERC-20** tokens you want to bridge in the **From** box.
3. Press **Move funds**.
4. Follow the prompts from your Web3 wallet.

> **Ensure sufficient ETH balance**
>
> Please ensure you have sufficient **ETH** in your wallet to cover the transaction costs; otherwise, no Web3 wallet pop-up will appear.

![Enter the amount of token to withdraw](/img/arb-bridge-getting-started-users-8.png)

A countdown will appear stating that you'll receive your funds in 7-8 days.

You can check the status of your withdrawal by clicking on your profile in the top-right corner and opening the **Transactions** tab, where you can claim it when it's ready.

![See the transaction history](/img/arb-bridge-getting-started-users-9.png)

Once the countdown is complete, press the **Claim** button to receive your funds.

## See also [#see-also]

- [USDC on Arbitrum One](/arbitrum-bridge/usdc-arbitrum-one)
- [Arbitrum bridge: Troubleshooting](/arbitrum-bridge/troubleshooting)
- [Arbitrum embedded bridge widget](/arbitrum-bridge/embedded-bridge-widget)
- [Bridge transaction traceability](/arbitrum-bridge/bridge-transaction-traceability)
- [How token bridging works (deep dive)](/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/token-bridging)
- [Bridge tokens programmatically](/arbitrum-essentials/bridging/overview)

The team working on Arbitrum is always interested and looking forward to engaging with its users. Why not follow us on [X (Twitter)](https://x.com/arbitrum) or join our community on [Discord](https://discord.gg/arbitrum)?

# Upcoming changes to transaction submission (/notices/transaction-submission-changes-notice)

We are changing how two transaction submission methods respond on Arbitrum chains. After the change, `eth_sendRawTransaction` and `eth_sendRawTransactionSync` will both return sooner than they do today. The changes are not live yet. We are posting this notice now so you have time to prepare. At this time, the precise latency gains/wins are unavailable; as soon as development and testing is complete, this page will be updated with this information.

> **What this means for you**
>
> - If you treat an `eth_sendRawTransaction` response as “**received**” and confirm the result later, you don’t need to change anything. You will get the transaction hash sooner.
> - If you treat an `eth_sendRawTransaction` response as “**included**,” or you retry based on the errors it returns, switch to `eth_sendRawTransactionSync`.
> - `eth_sendRawTransactionSync` will return sooner than it does today, but will no longer return the `blockHash` in the receipt (it will be `0x000...000` instead). If you need the `blockHash` in a receipt, continue polling `eth_getTransactionReceipt` from your own node or from a third-party RPC provider.
> - The node you send transactions to using `eth_sendRawTransactionSync` must run an upgraded Nitro version (version TBD). This applies to your own nodes and to third-party RPC providers.
>
> We will also be coordinating the change and neccesary upgrade with major RPC providers.

## Why this is happening [#why-this-is-happening]

These changes are part of our work to optimize Arbitrum chains for decentralized finance (DeFi). These changes are aimed at reducing the round-trip time to learn about when the sequencer receives or executes your transaction.

These updates will help teams who rely on speed, like traders, DeFi app developers, market makers, arbitrageurs, and solvers. By letting you know your transaction status faster, you can act faster, whether that means making your next trade or filling an order sooner. Ultimately, this should help you use your capital more efficiently, reduce trade time, and create better pricing for everyone.

## What’s changing [#whats-changing]

| Method                       | Returns today                                                                              | Returns after the change                                                                                                         |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `eth_sendRawTransaction`     | The transaction hash when the block is sealed, pre-check errors, or block inclusion errors | The transaction hash when it enters the sequencer's queue or pre-check errors. Inclusion errors will no longer be returned.      |
| `eth_sendRawTransactionSync` | A full receipt when a block is sealed, pre-check errors, or block inclusion errors         | A partial receipt (`blockHash` set to `0x000…000`) when the transaction is executed, pre-check errors, or block inclusion errors |

### `eth_sendRawTransaction` returns on admission to the queue [#eth_sendrawtransaction-returns-on-admission-to-the-queue]

`eth_sendRawTransaction` returns a response when the transaction enters the sequencer’s queue. It no longer waits for the sequencer to execute the transaction and include it in a block. This matches how the method behaves on other EVM chains, such as Ethereum, Base, Monad, and Polygon.

The sequencer will complete prechecks before admitting a transaction. These errors still return synchronously:

- Nonce already used
- Insufficient funds
- Fee cap
- Queue full

> **Some failed transactions no longer return an error**
>
> A transaction can pass the prechecks but still fail at block time. Examples are a nonce gap, a fee cap below the base fee, or a queue timeout. After the change, `eth_sendRawTransaction` no longer returns an error for these errors. Transactions that get dropped will not produce a receipt (unchanged from today's behavior).
>
> If your path depends on these inclusion-time errors, use `eth_sendRawTransactionSync` instead.

### `eth_sendRawTransactionSync` returns the receipt after execution [#eth_sendrawtransactionsync-returns-the-receipt-after-execution]

`eth_sendRawTransactionSync` will return the transaction receipt as soon as the sequencer finishes executing the transaction. It no longer waits for the block to finish building. It returns sooner than `eth_sendRawTransactionSync` and `eth_sendRawTransaction` does today.

> **Rare cases to be aware of**
>
> These could occur in a very small window between transaction execution and the block being sealed. If you have concerns about these rare cases, it may be best not to rely on this method and instead use polling.
>
> - Similar to the fast feed, a receipt can be retracted. A block can still fail after the sequencer executes a transaction, for example because of a disk write error or a sequencer crash. To avoid these cases, or to get the `blockHash`, poll `eth_getTransactionReceipt` for the canonical receipt.

## Who benefits [#who-benefits]

| If you currently…                                                                                                                                               | After the change…                                                                                                                                                           | Action required to get the benefit                                        |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Treat an `eth_sendRawTransaction` response as "received," then confirm through a receipt, the sequencer feed, or a nonce check | You benefit! You will get the transaction hash sooner compared to today                                                                                                     | None                                                                      |
| Poll `eth_getTransactionReceipt` and don't need the `blockHash`                                                                                                 | You benefit! The `eth_sendRawTransactionSync` method returns the status and logs in one call sooner than it does today & sooner than it would take if you continued to poll | Switch to `eth_sendRawTransactionSync`                                    |
| Submit user operations through the ZeroDev UltraRelay bundler                                                                                                   | You benefit! You will get user operation receipts sooner than before                                                                                                        | None                                                                      |
| Run custom logic or infrastructure to serve `eth_sendRawTransactionSync` calls                                                                                  | You benefit! The Nitro node serves these calls natively, removing the need to maintain and build custom logic for this method                                               | Upgrade Nitro to 3.14.x (not yet released), then retire your custom setup |
| Treat an `eth_sendRawTransaction` response as "included," or retry based on its errors                                                                          | You can no longer rely on `eth_sendRawTransaction` to report inclusion-time errors                                                                                          | Switch to `eth_sendRawTransactionSync`                                    |
| Need the canonical receipt with the `blockHash`                                                                                                                 | You will no longer get the `blockHash` in the receipt from `eth_sendRawTransactionSync`                                                                                     | Keep polling `eth_getTransactionReceipt`                                  |

> **Chains with more than one PGA round per block**
>
> The latency gain is larger on a chain that runs more than one Priority Gas Auction (PGA) round per block. Today, `eth_sendRawTransactionSync` waits for every round in the block to finish before it returns the receipt. After the change, it returns as soon as the sequencer executes your transaction, however many rounds remain.

> **If you run custom logic or infrastructure serving eth_sendRawTransactionSync**
>
> If you take no action, you can still serve `eth_sendRawTransactionSync` calls but they will not benefit from being faster or match the expected behaviors above.

## Actions required for node operators [#actions-required-for-node-operators]

The `eth_sendRawTransactionSync` change takes effect only on nodes that run the upgraded Nitro version (3.14.x). The required version is not released yet. We will update this notice with the version, Docker image, and release notes.

- If you run your own node, upgrade it to the required Nitro version when it ships.
- If you use a third-party RPC provider, such as Alchemy, confirm that your provider has upgraded using the `web3_clientVersion` RPC method. Offchain is working with major RPC providers to upgrade their nodes and update their documentation.
